turns.answer:
Database: PostgreSQL — ACID transactions and a relational model fit inventory stock levels, warehouses, and reservations well.
Hosting: a managed container platform (e.g. AWS ECS Fargate or Render) backed by a managed Postgres (RDS/Supabase) — simple ops, scales with you.
Note: if you later need massive write throughput or global edge reads, revisit with DynamoDB/Redis; otherwise start simple.
turns.ask: We are starting a new inventory service. Which database and which hosting would you pick for it? Answer in three lines, no tickets yet.

turns.answer:
1. Overselling: concurrent stock deductions can race and sell more than available if reservations/locking aren't designed up front.
2. Stale data: inventory spread across warehouses/channels drifts unless sync and event ordering are handled.
3. Scope creep: inventory touches orders, fulfillment, and accounting, so boundaries blur and the service becomes a monolith.
turns.ask: List three risks of building it, one line each. No tickets.

turns.answer:
Dev A owns the core domain: data model, stock/reservation logic, and transactional consistency (the risky concurrency surface).
Dev B owns the API/integration layer: endpoints, auth, events, and the warehouse/channel sync adapters.
